# number_prefix - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/number_prefix/

## Expand description

This is a library for formatting numbers with numeric prefixes, such as turning “3000 metres” into “3 kilometres”, or “8705 bytes” into “8.5 KiB”.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The function [ NumberPrefix::decimal](https://docs.rs/enum.NumberPrefix.html#method.decimal)
returns either a pair of the resulting number and its prefix, or a
notice that the number was too small to have any prefix applied to it. For
example:

```
use number_prefix::NumberPrefix;
let amount = 8542_f32;
let result = match NumberPrefix::decimal(amount) {
    NumberPrefix::Standalone(bytes) => {
        format!("The file is {} bytes in size", bytes)
    }
    NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefix, n) => {
        format!("The file is {:.1} {}B in size", n, prefix)
    }
};
assert_eq!("The file is 8.5 kB in size", result);
```
The `{:.1}` part of the formatting string tells it to restrict the
output to only one decimal place. This value is calculated by repeatedly
dividing the number by 1000 until it becomes less than that, which in this
case results in 8.542, which gets rounded down. Because only one division
had to take place, the function also returns the decimal prefix `Kilo`,
which gets converted to its internationally-recognised symbol when
formatted as a string.

If the value is too small to have any prefixes applied to it — in this case, if it’s under 1000 — then the standalone value will be returned:

```
use number_prefix::NumberPrefix;
let amount = 705_f32;
let result = match NumberPrefix::decimal(amount) {
    NumberPrefix::Standalone(bytes) => {
        format!("The file is {} bytes in size", bytes)
    }
    NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefix, n) => {
        format!("The file is {:.1} {}B in size", n, prefix)
    }
};
assert_eq!("The file is 705 bytes in size", result);
```
In this particular example, the user expects different formatting for both bytes and kilobytes: while prefixed values are given more precision, there’s no point using anything other than whole numbers for just byte amounts. This is why the function pays attention to values without any prefixes — they often need to be special-cased.

[§](https://docs.rs#binary-prefixes)Binary Prefixes

This library also allows you to use the *binary prefixes*, which use the
number 1024 (210) as the multiplier, rather than the more common 1000
(103). This uses the
[ NumberPrefix::binary](https://docs.rs/enum.NumberPrefix.html#method.binary) function.
For example:

```
use number_prefix::NumberPrefix;
let amount = 8542_f32;
let result = match NumberPrefix::binary(amount) {
    NumberPrefix::Standalone(bytes) => {
        format!("The file is {} bytes in size", bytes)
    }
    NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefix, n) => {
        format!("The file is {:.1} {}B in size", n, prefix)
    }
};
assert_eq!("The file is 8.3 KiB in size", result);
```
A kibibyte is slightly larger than a kilobyte, so the number is smaller in the result; but other than that, it works in exactly the same way, with the binary prefix being converted to a symbol automatically.

[§](https://docs.rs#which-type-of-prefix-should-i-use)Which type of prefix should I use?

There is no correct answer this question! Common practice is to use
the binary prefixes for numbers of *bytes*, while still using the decimal
prefixes for everything else. Computers work with powers of two, rather than
powers of ten, and by using the binary prefixes, you get a more accurate
representation of the amount of data.

[§](https://docs.rs#prefix-names)Prefix Names

If you need to describe your unit in actual words, rather than just with the
symbol, use one of the `upper`, `caps`, `lower`, or `symbol`, which output the
prefix in a variety of formats. For example:

```
use number_prefix::NumberPrefix;
let amount = 8542_f32;
let result = match NumberPrefix::decimal(amount) {
    NumberPrefix::Standalone(bytes) => {
        format!("The file is {} bytes in size", bytes)
    }
    NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefix, n) => {
        format!("The file is {:.1} {}bytes in size", n, prefix.lower())
    }
};
assert_eq!("The file is 8.5 kilobytes in size", result);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#string-parsing)String Parsing

There is a `FromStr` implementation for `NumberPrefix` that parses
strings containing numbers and trailing prefixes, such as `7.5E`.

Currently, the only supported units are `b` and `B` for bytes, and `m` for
metres. Whitespace is allowed between the number and the rest of the string.

```
use number_prefix::{NumberPrefix, Prefix};
assert_eq!("7.05E".parse::<NumberPrefix<_>>(),
           Ok(NumberPrefix::Prefixed(Prefix::Exa, 7.05_f64)));
assert_eq!("7.05".parse::<NumberPrefix<_>>(),
           Ok(NumberPrefix::Standalone(7.05_f64)));
assert_eq!("7.05 GiB".parse::<NumberPrefix<_>>(),
           Ok(NumberPrefix::Prefixed(Prefix::Gibi, 7.05_f64)));
```
## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Number](https://docs.rs/enum.NumberPrefix.html)- Prefix
- The result of trying to apply a prefix to a floating-point value.
- [Prefix](https://docs.rs/enum.Prefix.html)
- A numeric prefix, either binary or decimal.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Amounts](https://docs.rs/trait.Amounts.html)
- Traits for floating-point values for both the possible multipliers. They need to be Copy, have defined 1000 and 1024s, and implement a bunch of operators.

# number_prefix 0.4.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/number_prefix/latest

This is a library for formatting numbers with numeric prefixes, such as turning “3000 metres” into “3 kilometres”, or “8705 bytes” into “8.5 KiB”.

# Usage

The function [ NumberPrefix::decimal](https://docs.rs/enum.NumberPrefix.html#method.decimal)
returns either a pair of the resulting number and its prefix, or a
notice that the number was too small to have any prefix applied to it. For
example:

```
use NumberPrefix;
let amount = 8542_f32;
let result = match decimal ;
assert_eq!;
```
The `{:.1}` part of the formatting string tells it to restrict the
output to only one decimal place. This value is calculated by repeatedly
dividing the number by 1000 until it becomes less than that, which in this
case results in 8.542, which gets rounded down. Because only one division
had to take place, the function also returns the decimal prefix `Kilo`,
which gets converted to its internationally-recognised symbol when
formatted as a string.

If the value is too small to have any prefixes applied to it — in this case, if it’s under 1000 — then the standalone value will be returned:

```

let amount = 705_f32;
let result = match decimal ;
assert_eq!;
```
In this particular example, the user expects different formatting for both bytes and kilobytes: while prefixed values are given more precision, there’s no point using anything other than whole numbers for just byte amounts. This is why the function pays attention to values without any prefixes — they often need to be special-cased.

## Binary Prefixes

This library also allows you to use the *binary prefixes*, which use the
number 1024 (210) as the multiplier, rather than the more common 1000
(103). This uses the
[ NumberPrefix::binary](https://docs.rs/enum.NumberPrefix.html#method.binary) function.
For example:

```
use NumberPrefix;
let amount = 8542_f32;
let result = match binary ;
assert_eq!;
```
A kibibyte is slightly larger than a kilobyte, so the number is smaller in the result; but other than that, it works in exactly the same way, with the binary prefix being converted to a symbol automatically.

## Which type of prefix should I use?

There is no correct answer this question! Common practice is to use
the binary prefixes for numbers of *bytes*, while still using the decimal
prefixes for everything else. Computers work with powers of two, rather than
powers of ten, and by using the binary prefixes, you get a more accurate
representation of the amount of data.

## Prefix Names

If you need to describe your unit in actual words, rather than just with the
symbol, use one of the `upper`, `caps`, `lower`, or `symbol`, which output the
prefix in a variety of formats. For example:

```
use NumberPrefix;
let amount = 8542_f32;
let result = match decimal ;
assert_eq!;
```
## String Parsing

There is a `FromStr` implementation for `NumberPrefix` that parses
strings containing numbers and trailing prefixes, such as `7.5E`.

Currently, the only supported units are `b` and `B` for bytes, and `m` for
metres. Whitespace is allowed between the number and the rest of the string.

```
use ;
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/number_prefix/latest/target-redirect/number_prefix/

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

---

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

agnix-mcp-0.37.0 is not a library.

                MCP server for agnix - AI agent config linter

Exposes agnix validation as MCP tools for AI assistants.

## MCP Best Practices Implemented

- **Clear tool descriptions**: Each tool has a detailed description explaining what it does, when to use it, and what it returns
- **Rich parameter schemas**: All parameters have descriptions with examples
- **Structured outputs**: Returns JSON with predictable schema for easy parsing
- **Error handling**: Proper error messages with context
- **Server metadata**: Provides name, version, and usage instructions

# synth_backend_aarch64 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/synth-backend-aarch64/0.24.0/synth_backend_aarch64/

## Expand description

AArch64 (A64) host-native backend for synth — **milestone 1** (#538).

Goal (from #538): a minimal A64 integer-subset backend reachable via
`-b aarch64`, so synth output runs and debugs natively on arm64 dev hosts
(Apple Silicon, arm64 Linux/CI) instead of only under QEMU/Renode — and so a
third backend becomes a third differential oracle against the Thumb-2 and RV32
lowerings.

[§](https://docs.rs#milestone-status)Milestone status

- **1a (this crate, now):**the verified A64- *encoder*(integer data-processing +- `movz`/- `movk`+- `ret`, cross-checked against- `clang`) and a minimal straight-line- *selector*(params in- `w0..w7`, i32 add/sub/mul/and/or/xor + const, result to- `w0`,- `ret`).- `compile_bytes`turns a leaf integer function’s wasm ops into A64 machine code. Ops outside the subset return- `Unsupported`— an honest loud-skip, never wrong code.
- **1b (next):**an- `EM_AARCH64`relocatable-ELF emitter, the- `Backend`trait impl,- `-b aarch64`CLI wiring, and the native differential-execution acceptance probe (- `synth compile add.wat -b aarch64`→ link + run on the arm64 host, diff vs wasmtime).
- **later:**spilling, i64, floats, memory, control flow, calls, DWARF.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use backend::`- [AArch64Backend](https://docs.rs/backend/struct.AArch64Backend.html);
- `pub use selector::`- [SelectError](https://docs.rs/selector/struct.SelectError.html);
- `pub use selector::`- [select](https://docs.rs/selector/fn.select.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [backend](https://docs.rs/backend/index.html)
- `Backend`trait implementation for the AArch64 host-native backend (#538).
- [elf](https://docs.rs/elf/index.html)
- Minimal `EM_AARCH64`ELF64 relocatable-object emitter — milestone-1b (#538).
- [encoder](https://docs.rs/encoder/index.html)
- Minimal AArch64 (A64) instruction encoder — milestone-1 integer subset (#538).
- [selector](https://docs.rs/selector/index.html)
- Minimal AArch64 instruction selector — milestone-1 integer subset (#538).

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [compile_](https://docs.rs/fn.compile_bytes.html)- bytes
- Lower a single leaf integer function (wasm ops + declared param count) to A64
machine-code bytes (little-endian 32-bit words). Convenience over
`selector::select``.text`bytes.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Decoded](https://docs.rs/struct.DecodedModule.html)- Module
- Decoded WASM module with functions and memory
- [Function](https://docs.rs/struct.FunctionOps.html)- Ops
- Decoded function with its WasmOp sequence
- [Synthesis](https://docs.rs/struct.SynthesisEngine.html)- Engine
- [Wasm](https://docs.rs/struct.WasmGlobal.html)- Global
- A WASM global’s declaration — its initial value and mutability (#237).
Needed so the native-pointer ABI can recognize a global whose initializer is
a linear-memory address (e.g. `$__stack_pointer = 65536`) and make it`__synth_wasm_data`-relative, rather than reading it from an R9 globals table the self-contained drop-in object can’t rely on.
- [Wasm](https://docs.rs/struct.WasmMemory.html)- Memory
- WASM linear memory specification

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [WasmOp](https://docs.rs/enum.WasmOp.html)
- WebAssembly operation patterns Note: Cannot derive Eq because f32/f64 don’t implement Eq (NaN != NaN)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_wasm_functions.html)- wasm_ - functions
- Decode a WASM binary and extract all function bodies as WasmOp sequences
- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_wasm_module.html)- wasm_ - module
- Decode a WASM binary and extract functions, memory, and data segments

- **Cleanup Passes**: Remove dead/redundant code

- Constant Folding
- Common Subexpression Elimination (CSE)

# gravity_proto - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/gravity_proto/0.11.0/gravity_proto/

## Expand description

This crate provides Gravity proto definitions in Rust and also re-exports cosmos_sdk_proto for use by downstream crates. By default around a dozen proto files are generated and places into the prost folder. We could then proceed to fix up all these files and use them as the required dependencies to the Gravity file, but we chose instead to replace those paths with references ot upstream cosmos-sdk-proto and delete the other files. This reduces cruft in this repo even if it does make for a somewhat more confusing proto generation process.

# synth_cfg - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/synth-cfg/0.24.0/synth_cfg/

## Expand description

Control Flow Graph (CFG) for WebAssembly Functions

This crate provides CFG construction and analysis for WebAssembly functions, enabling proper branch target resolution and optimization.

[§](https://docs.rs#key-concepts)Key Concepts

- **Basic Block**: A maximal sequence of instructions with single entry and exit
- **CFG Edge**: Control flow from one basic block to another
- **Dominance**: Block A dominates B if all paths to B go through A
- **Loop**: A strongly connected component in the CFG

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Basic](https://docs.rs/struct.BasicBlock.html)- Block
- A basic block in the CFG
- [Cfg](https://docs.rs/struct.Cfg.html)
- Control Flow Graph
- [CfgBuilder](https://docs.rs/struct.CfgBuilder.html)
- Builder for constructing CFGs
- [Loop](https://docs.rs/struct.Loop.html)
- Loop information

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [BlockId](https://docs.rs/type.BlockId.html)
- Block identifier

# agnix_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/agnix-core/0.37.0/agnix_core/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#agnix-core)agnix-core

Core validation engine for agent configurations.

Validates:

- Agent Skills (SKILL.md)
- Agent definitions (.md files with frontmatter)
- MCP tool configurations
- Claude Code hooks
- CLAUDE.md memory files
- Plugin manifests

This crate requires `std`. The `filesystem` Cargo feature (enabled by
default) adds file I/O dependencies; disabling it does not enable `no_std`.

[§](https://docs.rs#stability-tiers)Stability Tiers

Public modules are classified into stability tiers:

- **Stable**–- `config`,- `diagnostics`,- `fixes`,- `fs`. These modules follow semver: breaking changes require a major version bump.
- **Unstable**–- `authoring`,- `eval`,- `i18n`,- `validation`. Interfaces may change on minor releases. Use with care in downstream crates.
- **Internal**–- `parsers`(pub(crate)). Not part of the public API. Some types are re-exported at the crate root with- `#[doc(hidden)]`for fuzz/bench/test use only.

# number_prefix 0.4.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/number_prefix/0.4.0

This is a library for formatting numbers with numeric prefixes, such as turning “3000 metres” into “3 kilometres”, or “8705 bytes” into “8.5 KiB”.

# Usage

The function [ NumberPrefix::decimal](https://docs.rs/enum.NumberPrefix.html#method.decimal)
returns either a pair of the resulting number and its prefix, or a
notice that the number was too small to have any prefix applied to it. For
example:

```
use NumberPrefix;
let amount = 8542_f32;
let result = match decimal ;
assert_eq!;
```
The `{:.1}` part of the formatting string tells it to restrict the
output to only one decimal place. This value is calculated by repeatedly
dividing the number by 1000 until it becomes less than that, which in this
case results in 8.542, which gets rounded down. Because only one division
had to take place, the function also returns the decimal prefix `Kilo`,
which gets converted to its internationally-recognised symbol when
formatted as a string.

If the value is too small to have any prefixes applied to it — in this case, if it’s under 1000 — then the standalone value will be returned:

```
use NumberPrefix;
let amount = 705_f32;
let result = match decimal ;
assert_eq!;
```
In this particular example, the user expects different formatting for both bytes and kilobytes: while prefixed values are given more precision, there’s no point using anything other than whole numbers for just byte amounts. This is why the function pays attention to values without any prefixes — they often need to be special-cased.

## Binary Prefixes

This library also allows you to use the *binary prefixes*, which use the
number 1024 (210) as the multiplier, rather than the more common 1000
(103). This uses the
[ NumberPrefix::binary](https://docs.rs/enum.NumberPrefix.html#method.binary) function.
For example:

```
use NumberPrefix;
let amount = 8542_f32;
let result = match binary ;
assert_eq!;
```
A kibibyte is slightly larger than a kilobyte, so the number is smaller in the result; but other than that, it works in exactly the same way, with the binary prefix being converted to a symbol automatically.

## Which type of prefix should I use?

There is no correct answer this question! Common practice is to use
the binary prefixes for numbers of *bytes*, while still using the decimal
prefixes for everything else. Computers work with powers of two, rather than
powers of ten, and by using the binary prefixes, you get a more accurate
representation of the amount of data.

## Prefix Names

If you need to describe your unit in actual words, rather than just with the
symbol, use one of the `upper`, `caps`, `lower`, or `symbol`, which output the
prefix in a variety of formats. For example:

```
use NumberPrefix;
let amount = 8542_f32;
let result = match decimal ;
assert_eq!;
```
## String Parsing

There is a `FromStr` implementation for `NumberPrefix` that parses
strings containing numbers and trailing prefixes, such as `7.5E`.

Currently, the only supported units are `b` and `B` for bytes, and `m` for
metres. Whitespace is allowed between the number and the rest of the string.

```
use ;
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```

# number_prefix - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/number_prefix/0.4.0/target-redirect/number_prefix/

## Expand description

This is a library for formatting numbers with numeric prefixes, such as turning “3000 metres” into “3 kilometres”, or “8705 bytes” into “8.5 KiB”.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The function [ NumberPrefix::decimal](https://docs.rs/enum.NumberPrefix.html#method.decimal)
returns either a pair of the resulting number and its prefix, or a
notice that the number was too small to have any prefix applied to it. For
example:

```
use number_prefix::NumberPrefix;
let amount = 8542_f32;
let result = match NumberPrefix::decimal(amount) {
    NumberPrefix::Standalone(bytes) => {
        format!("The file is {} bytes in size", bytes)
    }
    NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefix, n) => {
        format!("The file is {:.1} {}B in size", n, prefix)
    }
};
assert_eq!("The file is 8.5 kB in size", result);
```
The `{:.1}` part of the formatting string tells it to restrict the
output to only one decimal place. This value is calculated by repeatedly
dividing the number by 1000 until it becomes less than that, which in this
case results in 8.542, which gets rounded down. Because only one division
had to take place, the function also returns the decimal prefix `Kilo`,
which gets converted to its internationally-recognised symbol when
formatted as a string.

If the value is too small to have any prefixes applied to it — in this case, if it’s under 1000 — then the standalone value will be returned:

```
use number_prefix::NumberPrefix;
let amount = 705_f32;
let result = match NumberPrefix::decimal(amount) {
    NumberPrefix::Standalone(bytes) => {
        format!("The file is {} bytes in size", bytes)
    }
    NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefix, n) => {
        format!("The file is {:.1} {}B in size", n, prefix)
    }
};
assert_eq!("The file is 705 bytes in size", result);
```
In this particular example, the user expects different formatting for both bytes and kilobytes: while prefixed values are given more precision, there’s no point using anything other than whole numbers for just byte amounts. This is why the function pays attention to values without any prefixes — they often need to be special-cased.

[§](https://docs.rs#binary-prefixes)Binary Prefixes

This library also allows you to use the *binary prefixes*, which use the
number 1024 (210) as the multiplier, rather than the more common 1000
(103). This uses the
[ NumberPrefix::binary](https://docs.rs/enum.NumberPrefix.html#method.binary) function.
For example:

```
use number_prefix::NumberPrefix;
let amount = 8542_f32;
let result = match NumberPrefix::binary(amount) {
    NumberPrefix::Standalone(bytes) => {
        format!("The file is {} bytes in size", bytes)
    }
    NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefix, n) => {
        format!("The file is {:.1} {}B in size", n, prefix)
    }
};
assert_eq!("The file is 8.3 KiB in size", result);
```
A kibibyte is slightly larger than a kilobyte, so the number is smaller in the result; but other than that, it works in exactly the same way, with the binary prefix being converted to a symbol automatically.

[§](https://docs.rs#which-type-of-prefix-should-i-use)Which type of prefix should I use?

There is no correct answer this question! Common practice is to use
the binary prefixes for numbers of *bytes*, while still using the decimal
prefixes for everything else. Computers work with powers of two, rather than
powers of ten, and by using the binary prefixes, you get a more accurate
representation of the amount of data.

[§](https://docs.rs#prefix-names)Prefix Names

If you need to describe your unit in actual words, rather than just with the
symbol, use one of the `upper`, `caps`, `lower`, or `symbol`, which output the
prefix in a variety of formats. For example:

```
use number_prefix::NumberPrefix;
let amount = 8542_f32;
let result = match NumberPrefix::decimal(amount) {
    NumberPrefix::Standalone(bytes) => {
        format!("The file is {} bytes in size", bytes)
    }
    NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefix, n) => {
        format!("The file is {:.1} {}bytes in size", n, prefix.lower())
    }
};
assert_eq!("The file is 8.5 kilobytes in size", result);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#string-parsing)String Parsing

There is a `FromStr` implementation for `NumberPrefix` that parses
strings containing numbers and trailing prefixes, such as `7.5E`.

Currently, the only supported units are `b` and `B` for bytes, and `m` for
metres. Whitespace is allowed between the number and the rest of the string.

```
use number_prefix::{NumberPrefix, Prefix};
assert_eq!("7.05E".parse::<NumberPrefix<_>>(),
           Ok(NumberPrefix::Prefixed(Prefix::Exa, 7.05_f64)));
assert_eq!("7.05".parse::<NumberPrefix<_>>(),
           Ok(NumberPrefix::Standalone(7.05_f64)));
assert_eq!("7.05 GiB".parse::<NumberPrefix<_>>(),
           Ok(NumberPrefix::Prefixed(Prefix::Gibi, 7.05_f64)));
```
## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Number](https://docs.rs/enum.NumberPrefix.html)- Prefix
- The result of trying to apply a prefix to a floating-point value.
- [Prefix](https://docs.rs/enum.Prefix.html)
- A numeric prefix, either binary or decimal.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Amounts](https://docs.rs/trait.Amounts.html)
- Traits for floating-point values for both the possible multipliers. They need to be Copy, have defined 1000 and 1024s, and implement a bunch of operators.

[167](https://docs.rs#167)/// A numeric prefix, either binary or decimal.
[168](https://docs.rs#168)#[derive(PartialEq, Eq, Clone, Copy, Debug)]
[169](https://docs.rs#169)pub enum Prefix {
[170](https://docs.rs#170)
[171](https://docs.rs#171)    /// _kilo_, 10<sup>3</sup> or 1000<sup>1</sup>.
[172](https://docs.rs#172)    /// From the Greek ‘χίλιοι’ (‘chilioi’), meaning ‘thousand’.
[173](https://docs.rs#173)    Kilo,
[174](https://docs.rs#174)
[175](https://docs.rs#175)    /// _mega_, 10<sup>6</sup> or 1000<sup>2</sup>.
[176](https://docs.rs#176)    /// From the Ancient Greek ‘μέγας’ (‘megas’), meaning ‘great’.
[177](https://docs.rs#177)    Mega,
[178](https://docs.rs#178)
[179](https://docs.rs#179)    /// _giga_, 10<sup>9</sup> or 1000<sup>3</sup>.
[180](https://docs.rs#180)    /// From the Greek ‘γίγας’ (‘gigas’), meaning ‘giant’.
[181](https://docs.rs#181)    Giga,
[182](https://docs.rs#182)
[183](https://docs.rs#183)    /// _tera_, 10<sup>12</sup> or 1000<sup>4</sup>.
[184](https://docs.rs#184)    /// From the Greek ‘τέρας’ (‘teras’), meaning ‘monster’.
[185](https://docs.rs#185)    Tera,
[186](https://docs.rs#186)
[187](https://docs.rs#187)    /// _peta_, 10<sup>15</sup> or 1000<sup>5</sup>.
[188](https://docs.rs#188)    /// From the Greek ‘πέντε’ (‘pente’), meaning ‘five’.
[189](https://docs.rs#189)    Peta,
[190](https://docs.rs#190)
[191](https://docs.rs#191)    /// _exa_, 10<sup>18</sup> or 1000<sup>6</sup>.
[192](https://docs.rs#192)    /// From the Greek ‘ἕξ’ (‘hex’), meaning ‘six’.
[193](https://docs.rs#193)    Exa,
[194](https://docs.rs#194)
[195](https://docs.rs#195)    /// _zetta_, 10<sup>21</sup> or 1000<sup>7</sup>.
[196](https://docs.rs#196)    /// From the Latin ‘septem’, meaning ‘seven’.
[197](https://docs.rs#197)    Zetta,
[198](https://docs.rs#198)
[199](https://docs.rs#199)    /// _yotta_, 10<sup>24</sup> or 1000<sup>8</sup>.
[200](https://docs.rs#200)    /// From the Green ‘οκτώ’ (‘okto’), meaning ‘eight’.
[201](https://docs.rs#201)    Yotta,
[202](https://docs.rs#202)
[203](https://docs.rs#203)    /// _kibi_, 2<sup>10</sup> or 1024<sup>1</sup>.
[204](https://docs.rs#204)    /// The binary version of _kilo_.
[205](https://docs.rs#205)    Kibi,
[206](https://docs.rs#206)
[207](https://docs.rs#207)    /// _mebi_, 2<sup>20</sup> or 1024<sup>2</sup>.
[208](https://docs.rs#208)    /// The binary version of _mega_.
[209](https://docs.rs#209)    Mebi,
[210](https://docs.rs#210)
[211](https://docs.rs#211)    /// _gibi_, 2<sup>30</sup> or 1024<sup>3</sup>.
[212](https://docs.rs#212)    /// The binary version of _giga_.
[213](https://docs.rs#213)    Gibi,
[214](https://docs.rs#214)
[215](https://docs.rs#215)    /// _tebi_, 2<sup>40</sup> or 1024<sup>4</sup>.
[216](https://docs.rs#216)    /// The binary version of _tera_.
[217](https://docs.rs#217)    Tebi,
[218](https://docs.rs#218)
[219](https://docs.rs#219)    /// _pebi_, 2<sup>50</sup> or 1024<sup>5</sup>.
[220](https://docs.rs#220)    /// The binary version of _peta_.
[221](https://docs.rs#221)    Pebi,
[222](https://docs.rs#222)
[223](https://docs.rs#223)    /// _exbi_, 2<sup>60</sup> or 1024<sup>6</sup>.
[224](https://docs.rs#224)    /// The binary version of _exa_.
[225](https://docs.rs#225)    Exbi,
[226](https://docs.rs#226)    // you can download exa binaries at https://exa.website/#installation
[227](https://docs.rs#227)
[228](https://docs.rs#228)    /// _zebi_, 2<sup>70</sup> or 1024<sup>7</sup>.
[229](https://docs.rs#229)    /// The binary version of _zetta_.
[230](https://docs.rs#230)    Zebi,
[231](https://docs.rs#231)
[232](https://docs.rs#232)    /// _yobi_, 2<sup>80</sup> or 1024<sup>8</sup>.
[233](https://docs.rs#233)    /// The binary version of _yotta_.
[234](https://docs.rs#234)    Yobi,
[235](https://docs.rs#235)}
[236](https://docs.rs#236)
[237](https://docs.rs#237)
[238](https://docs.rs#238)/// The result of trying to apply a prefix to a floating-point value.
[239](https://docs.rs#239)#[derive(PartialEq, Eq, Clone, Debug)]
[240](https://docs.rs#240)pub enum NumberPrefix<F> {
[241](https://docs.rs#241)
[242](https://docs.rs#242)	/// A **standalone** value is returned when the number is too small to
[243](https://docs.rs#243)	/// have any prefixes applied to it. This is commonly a special case, so
[244](https://docs.rs#244)	/// is handled separately.
[245](https://docs.rs#245)    Standalone(F),
[246](https://docs.rs#246)
[247](https://docs.rs#247)    /// A **prefixed** value *is* large enough for prefixes. This holds the
[248](https://docs.rs#248)    /// prefix, as well as the resulting value.
[249](https://docs.rs#249)    Prefixed(Prefix, F),
[250](https://docs.rs#250)}
[251](https://docs.rs#251)
[252](https://docs.rs#252)impl<F: Amounts> NumberPrefix<F> {
[253](https://docs.rs#253)
[254](https://docs.rs#254)    /// Formats the given floating-point number using **decimal** prefixes.
[255](https://docs.rs#255)    ///
[256](https://docs.rs#256)    /// This function accepts both `f32` and `f64` values. If you’re trying to
[257](https://docs.rs#257)    /// format an integer, you’ll have to cast it first.
[258](https://docs.rs#258)    ///
[259](https://docs.rs#259)    /// # Examples
[260](https://docs.rs#260)    ///
[261](https://docs.rs#261)    /// ```
[262](https://docs.rs#262)    /// use number_prefix::{Prefix, NumberPrefix};
[263](https://docs.rs#263)    ///
[264](https://docs.rs#264)    /// assert_eq!(NumberPrefix::decimal(1_000_000_000_f32),
[265](https://docs.rs#265)    ///            NumberPrefix::Prefixed(Prefix::Giga, 1_f32));
[266](https://docs.rs#266)    /// ```
[267](https://docs.rs#267)    pub fn decimal(amount: F) -> Self {
[268](https://docs.rs#268)        use self::Prefix::*;
[269](https://docs.rs#269)        Self::format_number(amount, Amounts::NUM_1000, [Kilo, Mega, Giga, Tera, Peta, Exa, Zetta, Yotta])
[270](https://docs.rs#270)    }
[271](https://docs.rs#271)
[272](https://docs.rs#272)    /// Formats the given floating-point number using **binary** prefixes.
[273](https://docs.rs#273)    ///
[274](https://docs.rs#274)    /// This function accepts both `f32` and `f64` values. If you’re trying to
[275](https://docs.rs#275)    /// format an integer, you’ll have to cast it first.
[276](https://docs.rs#276)    ///
[277](https://docs.rs#277)    /// # Examples
[278](https://docs.rs#278)    ///
[279](https://docs.rs#279)    /// ```
[280](https://docs.rs#280)    /// use number_prefix::{Prefix, NumberPrefix};
[281](https://docs.rs#281)    ///
[282](https://docs.rs#282)    /// assert_eq!(NumberPrefix::binary(1_073_741_824_f64),
[283](https://docs.rs#283)    ///            NumberPrefix::Prefixed(Prefix::Gibi, 1_f64));
[284](https://docs.rs#284)    /// ```
[285](https://docs.rs#285)    pub fn binary(amount: F) -> Self {
[286](https://docs.rs#286)        use self::Prefix::*;
[287](https://docs.rs#287)        Self::format_number(amount, Amounts::NUM_1024, [Kibi, Mebi, Gibi, Tebi, Pebi, Exbi, Zebi, Yobi])
[288](https://docs.rs#288)    }
[289](https://docs.rs#289)
[290](https://docs.rs#290)    fn format_number(mut amount: F, kilo: F, prefixes: [Prefix; 8]) -> Self {
[291](https://docs.rs#291)
[292](https://docs.rs#292)        // For negative numbers, flip it to positive, do the processing, then
[293](https://docs.rs#293)        // flip it back to negative again afterwards.
[294](https://docs.rs#294)        let was_negative = if amount.is_negative() { amount = -amount; true } else { false };
[295](https://docs.rs#295)
[296](https://docs.rs#296)        let mut prefix = 0;
[297](https://docs.rs#297)        while amount >= kilo && prefix < 8 {
[298](https://docs.rs#298)            amount = amount / kilo;
[299](https://docs.rs#299)            prefix += 1;
[300](https://docs.rs#300)        }
[301](https://docs.rs#301)
[302](https://docs.rs#302)        if was_negative {
[303](https://docs.rs#303)            amount = -amount;
[304](https://docs.rs#304)        }
[305](https://docs.rs#305)
[306](https://docs.rs#306)        if prefix == 0 {
[307](https://docs.rs#307)            NumberPrefix::Standalone(amount)
[308](https://docs.rs#308)        }
[309](https://docs.rs#309)        else {
[310](https://docs.rs#310)            NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefixes[prefix - 1], amount)
[311](https://docs.rs#311)        }
[312](https://docs.rs#312)    }
[313](https://docs.rs#313)}
[314](https://docs.rs#314)
[315](https://docs.rs#315)#[cfg(feature = "std")]
[316](https://docs.rs#316)impl fmt::Display for Prefix {
[317](https://docs.rs#317)	fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
[318](https://docs.rs#318)		write!(f, "{}", self.symbol())
[319](https://docs.rs#319)	}
[320](https://docs.rs#320)}
[321](https://docs.rs#321)
[322](https://docs.rs#322)impl Prefix {
[323](https://docs.rs#323)
[324](https://docs.rs#324)	/// Returns the name in uppercase, such as “KILO”.
[325](https://docs.rs#325)	///
[326](https://docs.rs#326)	/// # Examples
[327](https://docs.rs#327)	///
[328](https://docs.rs#328)	/// ```
[329](https://docs.rs#329)	/// use number_prefix::Prefix;
[330](https://docs.rs#330)	///
[331](https://docs.rs#331)	/// assert_eq!("GIGA", Prefix::Giga.upper());
[332](https://docs.rs#332)	/// assert_eq!("GIBI", Prefix::Gibi.upper());
[333](https://docs.rs#333)	/// ```
[334](https://docs.rs#334)    pub fn upper(self) -> &'static str {
[335](https://docs.rs#335)        use self::Prefix::*;
[336](https://docs.rs#336)        match self {
[337](https://docs.rs#337)            Kilo => "KILO",  Mega => "MEGA",  Giga  => "GIGA",   Tera  => "TERA",
[338](https://docs.rs#338)            Peta => "PETA",  Exa  => "EXA",   Zetta => "ZETTA",  Yotta => "YOTTA",
[339](https://docs.rs#339)            Kibi => "KIBI",  Mebi => "MEBI",  Gibi  => "GIBI",   Tebi  => "TEBI",
[340](https://docs.rs#340)            Pebi => "PEBI",  Exbi => "EXBI",  Zebi  => "ZEBI",   Yobi  => "YOBI",
[341](https://docs.rs#341)        }
[342](https://docs.rs#342)    }
[343](https://docs.rs#343)
[344](https://docs.rs#344)    /// Returns the name with the first letter capitalised, such as “Mega”.
[345](https://docs.rs#345)    ///
[346](https://docs.rs#346)	/// # Examples
[347](https://docs.rs#347)	///
[348](https://docs.rs#348)	/// ```
[349](https://docs.rs#349)	/// use number_prefix::Prefix;
[350](https://docs.rs#350)	///
[351](https://docs.rs#351)	/// assert_eq!("Giga", Prefix::Giga.caps());
[352](https://docs.rs#352)	/// assert_eq!("Gibi", Prefix::Gibi.caps());
[353](https://docs.rs#353)	/// ```
[354](https://docs.rs#354)    pub fn caps(self) -> &'static str {
[355](https://docs.rs#355)        use self::Prefix::*;
[356](https://docs.rs#356)        match self {
[357](https://docs.rs#357)            Kilo => "Kilo",  Mega => "Mega",  Giga  => "Giga",   Tera  => "Tera",
[358](https://docs.rs#358)            Peta => "Peta",  Exa  => "Exa",   Zetta => "Zetta",  Yotta => "Yotta",
[359](https://docs.rs#359)            Kibi => "Kibi",  Mebi => "Mebi",  Gibi  => "Gibi",   Tebi  => "Tebi",
[360](https://docs.rs#360)            Pebi => "Pebi",  Exbi => "Exbi",  Zebi  => "Zebi",   Yobi  => "Yobi",
[361](https://docs.rs#361)        }
[362](https://docs.rs#362)    }
[363](https://docs.rs#363)
[364](https://docs.rs#364)    /// Returns the name in lowercase, such as “giga”.
[365](https://docs.rs#365)    ///
[366](https://docs.rs#366)    /// # Examples
[367](https://docs.rs#367)    ///
[368](https://docs.rs#368)    /// ```
[369](https://docs.rs#369)    /// use number_prefix::Prefix;
[370](https://docs.rs#370)    ///
[371](https://docs.rs#371)    /// assert_eq!("giga", Prefix::Giga.lower());
[372](https://docs.rs#372)    /// assert_eq!("gibi", Prefix::Gibi.lower());
[373](https://docs.rs#373)    /// ```
[374](https://docs.rs#374)    pub fn lower(self) -> &'static str {
[375](https://docs.rs#375)        use self::Prefix::*;
[376](https://docs.rs#376)        match self {
[377](https://docs.rs#377)            Kilo => "kilo",  Mega => "mega",  Giga  => "giga",   Tera  => "tera",
[378](https://docs.rs#378)            Peta => "peta",  Exa  => "exa",   Zetta => "zetta",  Yotta => "yotta",
[379](https://docs.rs#379)            Kibi => "kibi",  Mebi => "mebi",  Gibi  => "gibi",   Tebi  => "tebi",
[380](https://docs.rs#380)            Pebi => "pebi",  Exbi => "exbi",  Zebi  => "zebi",   Yobi  => "yobi",
[381](https://docs.rs#381)        }
[382](https://docs.rs#382)    }
[383](https://docs.rs#383)
[384](https://docs.rs#384)    /// Returns the short-hand symbol, such as “T” (for “tera”).
[385](https://docs.rs#385)    ///
[386](https://docs.rs#386)	/// # Examples
[387](https://docs.rs#387)	///
[388](https://docs.rs#388)	/// ```
[389](https://docs.rs#389)	/// use number_prefix::Prefix;
[390](https://docs.rs#390)	///
[391](https://docs.rs#391)	/// assert_eq!("G",  Prefix::Giga.symbol());
[392](https://docs.rs#392)	/// assert_eq!("Gi", Prefix::Gibi.symbol());
[393](https://docs.rs#393)	/// ```
[394](https://docs.rs#394)    pub fn symbol(self) -> &'static str {
[395](https://docs.rs#395)        use self::Prefix::*;
[396](https://docs.rs#396)        match self {
[397](https://docs.rs#397)            Kilo => "k",   Mega => "M",   Giga  => "G",   Tera  => "T",
[398](https://docs.rs#398)            Peta => "P",   Exa  => "E",   Zetta => "Z",   Yotta => "Y",
[399](https://docs.rs#399)            Kibi => "Ki",  Mebi => "Mi",  Gibi  => "Gi",  Tebi  => "Ti",
[400](https://docs.rs#400)            Pebi => "Pi",  Exbi => "Ei",  Zebi  => "Zi",  Yobi  => "Yi",
[401](https://docs.rs#401)        }
[402](https://docs.rs#402)    }
[403](https://docs.rs#403)}
[404](https://docs.rs#404)
[405](https://docs.rs#405)/// Traits for floating-point values for both the possible multipliers. They
[406](https://docs.rs#406)/// need to be Copy, have defined 1000 and 1024s, and implement a bunch of
[407](https://docs.rs#407)/// operators.
[408](https://docs.rs#408)pub trait Amounts: Copy + Sized + PartialOrd + Div<Output=Self> + Neg<Output=Self> {
[409](https://docs.rs#409)
[410](https://docs.rs#410)    /// The constant representing 1000, for decimal prefixes.
[411](https://docs.rs#411)    const NUM_1000: Self;
[412](https://docs.rs#412)
[413](https://docs.rs#413)    /// The constant representing 1024, for binary prefixes.
[414](https://docs.rs#414)    const NUM_1024: Self;
[415](https://docs.rs#415)
[416](https://docs.rs#416)    /// Whether this number is negative.
[417](https://docs.rs#417)    /// This is used internally.
[418](https://docs.rs#418)    fn is_negative(self) -> bool;
[419](https://docs.rs#419)}
[420](https://docs.rs#420)
[421](https://docs.rs#421)impl Amounts for f32 {
[422](https://docs.rs#422)    const NUM_1000: Self = 1000_f32;
[423](https://docs.rs#423)    const NUM_1024: Self = 1024_f32;
[424](https://docs.rs#424)
[425](https://docs.rs#425)    fn is_negative(self) -> bool {
[426](https://docs.rs#426)        self.is_sign_negative()
[427](https://docs.rs#427)    }
[428](https://docs.rs#428)}
[429](https://docs.rs#429)
[430](https://docs.rs#430)impl Amounts for f64 {
[431](https://docs.rs#431)    const NUM_1000: Self = 1000_f64;
[432](https://docs.rs#432)    const NUM_1024: Self = 1024_f64;
[433](https://docs.rs#433)
[434](https://docs.rs#434)    fn is_negative(self) -> bool {
[435](https://docs.rs#435)        self.is_sign_negative()
[436](https://docs.rs#436)    }
[437](https://docs.rs#437)}

[543](https://docs.rs#543)    	           NumberPrefix::Prefixed(Prefix::Yotta, 1f64))
[544](https://docs.rs#544)    }

[551](https://docs.rs#551)		           NumberPrefix::Prefixed(Prefix::Yotta, 1000f64))

# NumberPrefix in number_prefix - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/number_prefix/0.4.0/number_prefix/enum.NumberPrefix.html

```
pub enum NumberPrefix<F> {
    Standalone(F),
    Prefixed(
```
[Prefix](https://docs.rs/enum.Prefix.html), F),
}## Expand description

The result of trying to apply a prefix to a floating-point value.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Standalone)

### Standalone(F)

A **standalone** value is returned when the number is too small to
have any prefixes applied to it. This is commonly a special case, so
is handled separately.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Prefixed)

### Prefixed([Prefix](https://docs.rs/enum.Prefix.html), F)

A **prefixed** value *is* large enough for prefixes. This holds the
prefix, as well as the resulting value.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/number_prefix/lib.rs.html#252-313)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-NumberPrefix%3CF%3E)### impl<F: [Amounts](https://docs.rs/trait.Amounts.html)> [NumberPrefix](https://docs.rs/enum.NumberPrefix.html)<F>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/number_prefix/lib.rs.html#252-313)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-NumberPrefix%3CF%3E)

### impl<F: [Amounts](https://docs.rs/trait.Amounts.html)> [NumberPrefix](https://docs.rs/enum.NumberPrefix.html)<F>

Formats the given floating-point number using **decimal** prefixes.

This function accepts both `f32` and `f64` values. If you’re trying to
format an integer, you’ll have to cast it first.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use number_prefix::{Prefix, NumberPrefix};
assert_eq!(NumberPrefix::decimal(1_000_000_000_f32),
           NumberPrefix::Prefixed(Prefix::Giga, 1_f32));
```
```
30fn main() {
31
32    // part one, decimal prefixes
33    let mut n = 1_f64;
34    for _ in 0 .. 8 {
35        n *= 1000_f64;
36
37        let decimal = format_prefix(NumberPrefix::decimal(n));
38        let binary  = format_prefix(NumberPrefix::binary(n));
39        println!("{:26} bytes is {} and {:10}", n, decimal, binary);
40    }
41
42    println!();
43
44    // part two, binary prefixes
45    let mut n = 1_f64;
46    for _ in 0 .. 8 {
47        n *= 1024_f64;
48
49        let decimal = format_prefix(NumberPrefix::decimal(n));
50        let binary  = format_prefix(NumberPrefix::binary(n));
51        println!("{:26} bytes is {} and {:10}", n, binary, decimal);
52    }
53}
```

# number_prefix - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/number_prefix/latest/number_prefix/

## Expand description

This is a library for formatting numbers with numeric prefixes, such as turning “3000 metres” into “3 kilometres”, or “8705 bytes” into “8.5 KiB”.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The function [ NumberPrefix::decimal](https://docs.rs/enum.NumberPrefix.html#method.decimal)
returns either a pair of the resulting number and its prefix, or a
notice that the number was too small to have any prefix applied to it. For
example:

```
use number_prefix::NumberPrefix;
let amount = 8542_f32;
let result = match NumberPrefix::decimal(amount) {
    NumberPrefix::Standalone(bytes) => {
        format!("The file is {} bytes in size", bytes)
    }
    NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefix, n) => {
        format!("The file is {:.1} {}B in size", n, prefix)
    }
};
assert_eq!("The file is 8.5 kB in size", result);
```
The `{:.1}` part of the formatting string tells it to restrict the
output to only one decimal place. This value is calculated by repeatedly
dividing the number by 1000 until it becomes less than that, which in this
case results in 8.542, which gets rounded down. Because only one division
had to take place, the function also returns the decimal prefix `Kilo`,
which gets converted to its internationally-recognised symbol when
formatted as a string.

If the value is too small to have any prefixes applied to it — in this case, if it’s under 1000 — then the standalone value will be returned:

```
use number_prefix::NumberPrefix;
let amount = 705_f32;
let result = match NumberPrefix::decimal(amount) {
    NumberPrefix::Standalone(bytes) => {
        format!("The file is {} bytes in size", bytes)
    }
    NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefix, n) => {
        format!("The file is {:.1} {}B in size", n, prefix)
    }
};
assert_eq!("The file is 705 bytes in size", result);
```
In this particular example, the user expects different formatting for both bytes and kilobytes: while prefixed values are given more precision, there’s no point using anything other than whole numbers for just byte amounts. This is why the function pays attention to values without any prefixes — they often need to be special-cased.

[§](https://docs.rs#binary-prefixes)Binary Prefixes

This library also allows you to use the *binary prefixes*, which use the
number 1024 (210) as the multiplier, rather than the more common 1000
(103). This uses the
[ NumberPrefix::binary](https://docs.rs/enum.NumberPrefix.html#method.binary) function.
For example:

```
use number_prefix::NumberPrefix;
let amount = 8542_f32;
let result = match NumberPrefix::binary(amount) {
    NumberPrefix::Standalone(bytes) => {
        format!("The file is {} bytes in size", bytes)
    }
    NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefix, n) => {
        format!("The file is {:.1} {}B in size", n, prefix)
    }
};
assert_eq!("The file is 8.3 KiB in size", result);
```
A kibibyte is slightly larger than a kilobyte, so the number is smaller in the result; but other than that, it works in exactly the same way, with the binary prefix being converted to a symbol automatically.

[§](https://docs.rs#which-type-of-prefix-should-i-use)Which type of prefix should I use?

There is no correct answer this question! Common practice is to use
the binary prefixes for numbers of *bytes*, while still using the decimal
prefixes for everything else. Computers work with powers of two, rather than
powers of ten, and by using the binary prefixes, you get a more accurate
representation of the amount of data.

[§](https://docs.rs#prefix-names)Prefix Names

If you need to describe your unit in actual words, rather than just with the
symbol, use one of the `upper`, `caps`, `lower`, or `symbol`, which output the
prefix in a variety of formats. For example:

```
use number_prefix::NumberPrefix;
let amount = 8542_f32;
let result = match NumberPrefix::decimal(amount) {
    NumberPrefix::Standalone(bytes) => {
        format!("The file is {} bytes in size", bytes)
    }
    NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefix, n) => {
        format!("The file is {:.1} {}bytes in size", n, prefix.lower())
    }
};
assert_eq!("The file is 8.5 kilobytes in size", result);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#string-parsing)String Parsing

There is a `FromStr` implementation for `NumberPrefix` that parses
strings containing numbers and trailing prefixes, such as `7.5E`.

Currently, the only supported units are `b` and `B` for bytes, and `m` for
metres. Whitespace is allowed between the number and the rest of the string.

```
use number_prefix::{NumberPrefix, Prefix};
assert_eq!("7.05E".parse::<NumberPrefix<_>>(),
           Ok(NumberPrefix::Prefixed(Prefix::Exa, 7.05_f64)));
assert_eq!("7.05".parse::<NumberPrefix<_>>(),
           Ok(NumberPrefix::Standalone(7.05_f64)));
assert_eq!("7.05 GiB".parse::<NumberPrefix<_>>(),
           Ok(NumberPrefix::Prefixed(Prefix::Gibi, 7.05_f64)));
```
## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Number](https://docs.rs/enum.NumberPrefix.html)- Prefix
- The result of trying to apply a prefix to a floating-point value.
- [Prefix](https://docs.rs/enum.Prefix.html)
- A numeric prefix, either binary or decimal.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Amounts](https://docs.rs/trait.Amounts.html)
- Traits for floating-point values for both the possible multipliers. They need to be Copy, have defined 1000 and 1024s, and implement a bunch of operators.

# number_prefix 0.3.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/number_prefix/0.3.0

This is a library for formatting numbers with numeric prefixes, such as turning “3000 metres” into “3 kilometres”, or “8705 bytes” into “8.5 KiB”.

# Installation

This crate works with [Cargo](http://crates.io). Add the following to your `Cargo.toml` dependencies section:

```
[]
 = "0.3"
```
This crate has `no_std` support. To activate it, disable the `std` Cargo feature.

# Usage

The function `NumberPrefix::decimal` returns either a pair of the resulting number and its prefix, or a notice that the number was too small to have any prefix applied to it.
For example:

```
use ;
match decimal
```
This will print out `"The file is 8.5 kB in size"`.
The `{:.0}` part of the formatting string tells it to restrict the output to only one decimal place.
This value is calculated by repeatedly dividing the number by 1000 until it becomes less than that, which in this case results in 8.542, which gets rounded down.
Because only one division had to take place, the function also returns the decimal prefix `Kilo`, which gets converted to its internationally-recognised symbol when formatted as a string.

If the value is too small to have any prefixes applied to it — in this case, if it’s under 1000 — then the standalone value will be returned:

```
use ;
match decimal
```
This will print out `"The file is 705 bytes in size"`, having chosen the other path to follow.
In this particular example, the user expects different formatting for both bytes and kilobytes: while prefixed values are given more precision, there’s no point using anything other than whole numbers for just byte amounts.
This is why the function pays attention to values without any prefixes — they often need to be special-cased.

## Binary Prefixes

This library also allows you to use the *binary prefixes*, which use the number 1024 (210) as the multiplier, rather than the more common 1000 (103).
This uses the `NumberPrefix::binary` function. For example:

```
use ;
match binary
```
This will print out `"The file is 8.3 KiB in size"`.
A kibibyte is slightly larger than a kilobyte, so the number is smaller in the result; but other than that, it works in exactly the same way, with the binary prefix being converted to a symbol automatically.

## Which type of prefix should I use?

There is no correct answer to this question!
Current practice is to use the binary prefixes for numbers of *bytes*, while still using the decimal prefixes for everything else.
Computers work with powers of two, rather than powers of ten, and by using the binary prefixes, you get a more accurate representation of the amount of data.

## Prefix Names

If you need to describe your unit in actual words, rather than just with
the symbol, import the `PrefixNames` trait, which adds methods to output
the prefix in a variety of formats. For example:

```
use ;
match decimal
```

## Prefix Names

If you need to describe your unit in actual words, rather than just with
the symbol, import the `PrefixNames` trait, which adds methods to output
the prefix in a variety of formats. For example:

```
use ;
match decimal_prefix
```

---

# number_prefix 0.2.7 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/number_prefix/0.2.7

This is a library for formatting numbers with numeric prefixes, such as turning “3000 metres” into “3 kilometres”, or “8705 bytes” into “8.5 KiB”.

# Installation

This crate works with [Cargo](http://crates.io). Add the following to your `Cargo.toml` dependencies section:

```
[]
 = "0.2.7"
```
# Usage

The function `decimal_prefix` returns either a pair of the resulting number and its prefix, or a notice that the number was too small to have any prefix applied to it.
For example:

```
use ;
match decimal_prefix
```
This will print out `"The file is 8.5 kB in size"`.
The `{:.0}` part of the formatting string tells it to restrict the output to only one decimal place.
This value is calculated by repeatedly dividing the number by 1000 until it becomes less than that, which in this case results in 8.542, which gets rounded down.
Because only one division had to take place, the function also returns the decimal prefix `Kilo`, which gets converted to its internationally-recognised symbol when formatted as a string.

If the value is too small to have any prefixes applied to it - in this case, if it’s under 1000 - then the standalone value will be returned:

```
use ;
match decimal_prefix
```
This will print out `"The file is 705 bytes in size"`, having chosen the other path to follow.
In this particular example, the user expects different formatting for both bytes and kilobytes: while prefixed values are given more precision, there’s no point using anything other than whole numbers for just byte amounts.
This is why the function pays attention to values without any prefixes - they often need to be special-cased.

## Binary Prefixes

This library also allows you to use the *binary prefixes*, which use the number 1024 (210) as the multiplier, rather than the more common 1000 (103).
This uses the `binary_prefix` function. For example:

```
use ;
match binary_prefix
```
This will print out `"The file is 8.3 KiB in size"`.
A kibibyte is slightly larger than a kilobyte, so the number is smaller in the result; but other than that, it works in exactly the same way, with the binary prefix being converted to a symbol automatically.

### Which type of prefix should I use?

There is no one way to answer this question!
The prevailing theory is to use the binary prefixes for numbers of *bytes*, while still using the decimal prefixes for everything else.
Computers work with powers of two, rather than powers of ten, and by using the binary prefixes, you get a more accurate representation about the amount of data.

## Prefix Names

If you need to describe your unit in actual words, rather than just with
the symbol, import the `PrefixNames` trait, which adds methods to output
the prefix in a variety of formats. For example:

```
use ;
match decimal_prefix
```

---

# number_prefix - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/number_prefix/latest/target-redirect/number_prefix/index.html

## Expand description

This is a library for formatting numbers with numeric prefixes, such as turning “3000 metres” into “3 kilometres”, or “8705 bytes” into “8.5 KiB”.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The function [ NumberPrefix::decimal](https://docs.rs/enum.NumberPrefix.html#method.decimal)
returns either a pair of the resulting number and its prefix, or a
notice that the number was too small to have any prefix applied to it. For
example:

```
use number_prefix::NumberPrefix;
let amount = 8542_f32;
let result = match NumberPrefix::decimal(amount) {
    NumberPrefix::Standalone(bytes) => {
        format!("The file is {} bytes in size", bytes)
    }
    NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefix, n) => {
        format!("The file is {:.1} {}B in size", n, prefix)
    }
};
assert_eq!("The file is 8.5 kB in size", result);
```
The `{:.1}` part of the formatting string tells it to restrict the
output to only one decimal place. This value is calculated by repeatedly
dividing the number by 1000 until it becomes less than that, which in this
case results in 8.542, which gets rounded down. Because only one division
had to take place, the function also returns the decimal prefix `Kilo`,
which gets converted to its internationally-recognised symbol when
formatted as a string.

If the value is too small to have any prefixes applied to it — in this case, if it’s under 1000 — then the standalone value will be returned:

```
use number_prefix::NumberPrefix;
let amount = 705_f32;
let result = match NumberPrefix::decimal(amount) {
    NumberPrefix::Standalone(bytes) => {
        format!("The file is {} bytes in size", bytes)
    }
    NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefix, n) => {
        format!("The file is {:.1} {}B in size", n, prefix)
    }
};
assert_eq!("The file is 705 bytes in size", result);
```
In this particular example, the user expects different formatting for both bytes and kilobytes: while prefixed values are given more precision, there’s no point using anything other than whole numbers for just byte amounts. This is why the function pays attention to values without any prefixes — they often need to be special-cased.

[§](https://docs.rs#binary-prefixes)Binary Prefixes

This library also allows you to use the *binary prefixes*, which use the
number 1024 (210) as the multiplier, rather than the more common 1000
(103). This uses the
[ NumberPrefix::binary](https://docs.rs/enum.NumberPrefix.html#method.binary) function.
For example:

```
use number_prefix::NumberPrefix;
let amount = 8542_f32;
let result = match NumberPrefix::binary(amount) {
    NumberPrefix::Standalone(bytes) => {
        format!("The file is {} bytes in size", bytes)
    }
    NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefix, n) => {
        format!("The file is {:.1} {}B in size", n, prefix)
    }
};
assert_eq!("The file is 8.3 KiB in size", result);
```
A kibibyte is slightly larger than a kilobyte, so the number is smaller in the result; but other than that, it works in exactly the same way, with the binary prefix being converted to a symbol automatically.

[§](https://docs.rs#which-type-of-prefix-should-i-use)Which type of prefix should I use?

There is no correct answer this question! Common practice is to use
the binary prefixes for numbers of *bytes*, while still using the decimal
prefixes for everything else. Computers work with powers of two, rather than
powers of ten, and by using the binary prefixes, you get a more accurate
representation of the amount of data.

[§](https://docs.rs#prefix-names)Prefix Names

If you need to describe your unit in actual words, rather than just with the
symbol, use one of the `upper`, `caps`, `lower`, or `symbol`, which output the
prefix in a variety of formats. For example:

```
use number_prefix::NumberPrefix;
let amount = 8542_f32;
let result = match NumberPrefix::decimal(amount) {
    NumberPrefix::Standalone(bytes) => {
        format!("The file is {} bytes in size", bytes)
    }
    NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefix, n) => {
        format!("The file is {:.1} {}bytes in size", n, prefix.lower())
    }
};
assert_eq!("The file is 8.5 kilobytes in size", result);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#string-parsing)String Parsing

There is a `FromStr` implementation for `NumberPrefix` that parses
strings containing numbers and trailing prefixes, such as `7.5E`.

Currently, the only supported units are `b` and `B` for bytes, and `m` for
metres. Whitespace is allowed between the number and the rest of the string.

```
use number_prefix::{NumberPrefix, Prefix};
assert_eq!("7.05E".parse::<NumberPrefix<_>>(),
           Ok(NumberPrefix::Prefixed(Prefix::Exa, 7.05_f64)));
assert_eq!("7.05".parse::<NumberPrefix<_>>(),
           Ok(NumberPrefix::Standalone(7.05_f64)));
assert_eq!("7.05 GiB".parse::<NumberPrefix<_>>(),
           Ok(NumberPrefix::Prefixed(Prefix::Gibi, 7.05_f64)));
```
## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Number](https://docs.rs/enum.NumberPrefix.html)- Prefix
- The result of trying to apply a prefix to a floating-point value.
- [Prefix](https://docs.rs/enum.Prefix.html)
- A numeric prefix, either binary or decimal.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Amounts](https://docs.rs/trait.Amounts.html)
- Traits for floating-point values for both the possible multipliers. They need to be Copy, have defined 1000 and 1024s, and implement a bunch of operators.

[169](https://docs.rs#169)pub enum Prefix {
[170](https://docs.rs#170)
[171](https://docs.rs#171)    /// _kilo_, 10<sup>3</sup> or 1000<sup>1</sup>.
[172](https://docs.rs#172)    /// From the Greek ‘χίλιοι’ (‘chilioi’), meaning ‘thousand’.
[173](https://docs.rs#173)    Kilo,
[174](https://docs.rs#174)
[175](https://docs.rs#175)    /// _mega_, 10<sup>6</sup> or 1000<sup>2</sup>.
[176](https://docs.rs#176)    /// From the Ancient Greek ‘μέγας’ (‘megas’), meaning ‘great’.
[177](https://docs.rs#177)    Mega,
[178](https://docs.rs#178)
[179](https://docs.rs#179)    /// _giga_, 10<sup>9</sup> or 1000<sup>3</sup>.
[180](https://docs.rs#180)    /// From the Greek ‘γίγας’ (‘gigas’), meaning ‘giant’.
[181](https://docs.rs#181)    Giga,
[182](https://docs.rs#182)
[183](https://docs.rs#183)    /// _tera_, 10<sup>12</sup> or 1000<sup>4</sup>.
[184](https://docs.rs#184)    /// From the Greek ‘τέρας’ (‘teras’), meaning ‘monster’.
[185](https://docs.rs#185)    Tera,
[186](https://docs.rs#186)
[187](https://docs.rs#187)    /// _peta_, 10<sup>15</sup> or 1000<sup>5</sup>.
[188](https://docs.rs#188)    /// From the Greek ‘πέντε’ (‘pente’), meaning ‘five’.
[189](https://docs.rs#189)    Peta,
[190](https://docs.rs#190)
[191](https://docs.rs#191)    /// _exa_, 10<sup>18</sup> or 1000<sup>6</sup>.
[192](https://docs.rs#192)    /// From the Greek ‘ἕξ’ (‘hex’), meaning ‘six’.
[193](https://docs.rs#193)    Exa,
[194](https://docs.rs#194)
[195](https://docs.rs#195)    /// _zetta_, 10<sup>21</sup> or 1000<sup>7</sup>.
[196](https://docs.rs#196)    /// From the Latin ‘septem’, meaning ‘seven’.
[197](https://docs.rs#197)    Zetta,
[198](https://docs.rs#198)
[199](https://docs.rs#199)    /// _yotta_, 10<sup>24</sup> or 1000<sup>8</sup>.
[200](https://docs.rs#200)    /// From the Green ‘οκτώ’ (‘okto’), meaning ‘eight’.
[201](https://docs.rs#201)    Yotta,
[202](https://docs.rs#202)
[203](https://docs.rs#203)    /// _kibi_, 2<sup>10</sup> or 1024<sup>1</sup>.
[204](https://docs.rs#204)    /// The binary version of _kilo_.
[205](https://docs.rs#205)    Kibi,
[206](https://docs.rs#206)
[207](https://docs.rs#207)    /// _mebi_, 2<sup>20</sup> or 1024<sup>2</sup>.
[208](https://docs.rs#208)    /// The binary version of _mega_.
[209](https://docs.rs#209)    Mebi,
[210](https://docs.rs#210)
[211](https://docs.rs#211)    /// _gibi_, 2<sup>30</sup> or 1024<sup>3</sup>.
[212](https://docs.rs#212)    /// The binary version of _giga_.
[213](https://docs.rs#213)    Gibi,
[214](https://docs.rs#214)
[215](https://docs.rs#215)    /// _tebi_, 2<sup>40</sup> or 1024<sup>4</sup>.
[216](https://docs.rs#216)    /// The binary version of _tera_.
[217](https://docs.rs#217)    Tebi,
[218](https://docs.rs#218)
[219](https://docs.rs#219)    /// _pebi_, 2<sup>50</sup> or 1024<sup>5</sup>.
[220](https://docs.rs#220)    /// The binary version of _peta_.
[221](https://docs.rs#221)    Pebi,
[222](https://docs.rs#222)
[223](https://docs.rs#223)    /// _exbi_, 2<sup>60</sup> or 1024<sup>6</sup>.
[224](https://docs.rs#224)    /// The binary version of _exa_.
[225](https://docs.rs#225)    Exbi,
[226](https://docs.rs#226)    // you can download exa binaries at https://exa.website/#installation
[227](https://docs.rs#227)
[228](https://docs.rs#228)    /// _zebi_, 2<sup>70</sup> or 1024<sup>7</sup>.
[229](https://docs.rs#229)    /// The binary version of _zetta_.
[230](https://docs.rs#230)    Zebi,

[238](https://docs.rs#238)/// The result of trying to apply a prefix to a floating-point value.
[239](https://docs.rs#239)#[derive(PartialEq, Eq, Clone, Debug)]
[240](https://docs.rs#240)pub enum NumberPrefix<F> {
[241](https://docs.rs#241)
[242](https://docs.rs#242)	/// A **standalone** value is returned when the number is too small to
[243](https://docs.rs#243)	/// have any prefixes applied to it. This is commonly a special case, so
[244](https://docs.rs#244)	/// is handled separately.
[245](https://docs.rs#245)    Standalone(F),
[246](https://docs.rs#246)
[247](https://docs.rs#247)    /// A **prefixed** value *is* large enough for prefixes. This holds the
[248](https://docs.rs#248)    /// prefix, as well as the resulting value.
[249](https://docs.rs#249)    Prefixed(Prefix, F),
[250](https://docs.rs#250)}
[251](https://docs.rs#251)
[252](https://docs.rs#252)impl<F: Amounts> NumberPrefix<F> {
[253](https://docs.rs#253)
[254](https://docs.rs#254)    /// Formats the given floating-point number using **decimal** prefixes.
[255](https://docs.rs#255)    ///
[256](https://docs.rs#256)    /// This function accepts both `f32` and `f64` values. If you’re trying to
[257](https://docs.rs#257)    /// format an integer, you’ll have to cast it first.
[258](https://docs.rs#258)    ///
[259](https://docs.rs#259)    /// # Examples
[260](https://docs.rs#260)    ///
[261](https://docs.rs#261)    /// ```
[262](https://docs.rs#262)    /// use number_prefix::{Prefix, NumberPrefix};
[263](https://docs.rs#263)    ///
[264](https://docs.rs#264)    /// assert_eq!(NumberPrefix::decimal(1_000_000_000_f32),
[265](https://docs.rs#265)    ///            NumberPrefix::Prefixed(Prefix::Giga, 1_f32));
[266](https://docs.rs#266)    /// ```
[267](https://docs.rs#267)    pub fn decimal(amount: F) -> Self {
[268](https://docs.rs#268)        use self::Prefix::*;
[269](https://docs.rs#269)        Self::format_number(amount, Amounts::NUM_1000, [Kilo, Mega, Giga, Tera, Peta, Exa, Zetta, Yotta])
[270](https://docs.rs#270)    }
[271](https://docs.rs#271)
[272](https://docs.rs#272)    /// Formats the given floating-point number using **binary** prefixes.
[273](https://docs.rs#273)    ///
[274](https://docs.rs#274)    /// This function accepts both `f32` and `f64` values. If you’re trying to
[275](https://docs.rs#275)    /// format an integer, you’ll have to cast it first.
[276](https://docs.rs#276)    ///
[277](https://docs.rs#277)    /// # Examples
[278](https://docs.rs#278)    ///
[279](https://docs.rs#279)    /// ```
[280](https://docs.rs#280)    /// use number_prefix::{Prefix, NumberPrefix};
[281](https://docs.rs#281)    ///
[282](https://docs.rs#282)    /// assert_eq!(NumberPrefix::binary(1_073_741_824_f64),
[283](https://docs.rs#283)    ///            NumberPrefix::Prefixed(Prefix::Gibi, 1_f64));
[284](https://docs.rs#284)    /// ```
[285](https://docs.rs#285)    pub fn binary(amount: F) -> Self {
[286](https://docs.rs#286)        use self::Prefix::*;
[287](https://docs.rs#287)        Self::format_number(amount, Amounts::NUM_1024, [Kibi, Mebi, Gibi, Tebi, Pebi, Exbi, Zebi, Yobi])
[288](https://docs.rs#288)    }
[289](https://docs.rs#289)
[290](https://docs.rs#290)    fn format_number(mut amount: F, kilo: F, prefixes: [Prefix; 8]) -> Self {
[291](https://docs.rs#291)
[292](https://docs.rs#292)        // For negative numbers, flip it to positive, do the processing, then
[293](https://docs.rs#293)        // flip it back to negative again afterwards.
[294](https://docs.rs#294)        let was_negative = if amount.is_negative() { amount = -amount; true } else { false };
[295](https://docs.rs#295)
[296](https://docs.rs#296)        let mut prefix = 0;
[297](https://docs.rs#297)        while amount >= kilo && prefix < 8 {
[298](https://docs.rs#298)            amount = amount / kilo;
[299](https://docs.rs#299)            prefix += 1;
[300](https://docs.rs#300)        }
[301](https://docs.rs#301)
[302](https://docs.rs#302)        if was_negative {
[303](https://docs.rs#303)            amount = -amount;
[304](https://docs.rs#304)        }
[305](https://docs.rs#305)
[306](https://docs.rs#306)        if prefix == 0 {
[307](https://docs.rs#307)            NumberPrefix::Standalone(amount)
[308](https://docs.rs#308)        }
[309](https://docs.rs#309)        else {
[310](https://docs.rs#310)            NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefixes[prefix - 1], amount)
[311](https://docs.rs#311)        }
[312](https://docs.rs#312)    }
[313](https://docs.rs#313)}
[314](https://docs.rs#314)
[315](https://docs.rs#315)#[cfg(feature = "std")]

[319](https://docs.rs#319)	}

[341](https://docs.rs#341)        }

[405](https://docs.rs#405)/// Traits for floating-point values for both the possible multipliers. They

[407](https://docs.rs#407)/// operators.

[409](https://docs.rs#409)

[412](https://docs.rs#412)

[414](https://docs.rs#414)    const NUM_1024: Self;
[415](https://docs.rs#415)
[416](https://docs.rs#416)    /// Whether this number is negative.
[417](https://docs.rs#417)    /// This is used internally.
[418](https://docs.rs#418)    fn is_negative(self) -> bool;
[419](https://docs.rs#419)}
